parts.text:
Calcium is an essential mineral that your body needs to build and maintain strong bones and teeth, ensure proper muscle and nerve function, and support heart health. The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for most adults is **1,000 mg to 1,200 mg of calcium per day**.

Here is a comprehensive list of calcium-rich foods, categorized by food group:

---

### 1. Dairy Products (Traditional Sources)
Dairy is the most well-known and easily absorbed source of dietary calcium.
*   **Yogurt (Plain, low-fat):** ~300–450 mg per cup (8 oz). Yogurt is also high in phosphorus, potassium, and beneficial probiotics.
*   **Milk (Whole, low-fat, or skim):** ~300 mg per cup (8 oz). 
*   **Cheese:** 
    *   *Parmesan:* ~330 mg per ounce (highly concentrated).
    *   *Cheddar, Swiss, Mozzarella:* ~200 mg per ounce.
    *   *Cottage Cheese:* ~138 mg per cup.

### 2. Plant-Based & Dairy-Free Sources
If you are vegan, lactose intolerant, or simply prefer plant-based foods, there are plenty of excellent non-dairy sources:
*   **Tofu (prepared with calcium sulfate):** ~200–800 mg per half-cup (check the label to ensure it was set using calcium).
*   **Chia Seeds:** ~180 mg per 2 tablespoons (approx. 1 ounce).
*   **Sesame Seeds (and Tahini):** ~88 mg per tablespoon.
*   **Almonds:** ~75 mg per ounce (about 23 whole almonds). Almonds have the highest calcium content among all nuts.
*   **White Beans (Navy, Great Northern):** ~120–140 mg per cup (cooked).
*   **Edamame:** ~98 mg per cup (cooked).

### 3. Leafy Greens and Vegetables
Dark leafy greens are excellent low-calorie sources of calcium, though some (like spinach) contain oxalates which can limit absorption. The best, most bioavailable leafy options are:
*   **Collard Greens (cooked):** ~268 mg per cup.
*   **Turnip Greens (cooked):** ~197 mg per cup.
*   **Kale (cooked):** ~180 mg per cup (or about 100 mg per cup raw).
*   **Bok Choy (Chinese cabbage):** ~160 mg per cup (cooked).
*   **Broccoli:** ~60 mg per cup (cooked).

### 4. Seafood (with Bones)
Fish that have edible, soft bones are incredibly rich in calcium.
*   **Sardines (canned with bones):** ~325 mg per 3 ounces.
*   **Canned Salmon (with bones):** ~180 mg per 3 ounces. (Regular fresh salmon also contains some calcium, but much less than canned salmon with bones).

### 5. Fortified Foods
Many everyday foods are heavily fortified with calcium to help people meet their daily goals.
*   **Fortified Plant Milks (Almond, Soy, Oat, Coconut):** ~300–450 mg per cup (comparable to or higher than cow’s milk; shake the carton well, as calcium can settle to the bottom).
*   **Fortified Orange Juice:** ~350 mg per cup.
*   **Fortified Ready-to-Eat Cereals:** Some can contain up to 1,000 mg (100% of the daily value) per serving, though 100–300 mg is more common. Check the nutrition facts panel.

---

### Tips for Maximizing Calcium Absorption
*   **Get enough Vitamin D:** Your body cannot properly absorb calcium without adequate levels of Vitamin D. You can get Vitamin D from sunlight, egg yolks, fatty fish, or supplements.
*   **Avoid over-consuming coffee/soda:** High intake of caffeine and phosphoric acid (found in many dark sodas) can interfere with calcium absorption and cause your body to lose calcium through urine.
*   **Note on "high-oxalate" greens:** Spinach, beet greens, and Swiss chard are high in calcium but also high in *oxalates*, compounds that bind to calcium and make it very difficult for your body to absorb. Use collard greens, kale, and bok choy for better calcium absorption.
